qs.q: Which specific finding is characteristic of occult filariasis resulting from a hypersensitivity reaction to filarial antigens?
qs.e: Occult filariasis is characterized by massive eosinophilia ranging from 30 to 80 percent because microfilariae are destroyed in tissues rather than circulating in blood. Elephantiasis is a feature of classical filariasis, not occult filariasis.

qs.q: Which diagnostic tool is noted as the simplest and most sensitive method for diagnosing malaria as well as conditions like babesiosis and filariasis?
qs.e: The QBC Malaria method has evolved as a rapid, precise, simple, and sensitive method for diagnosing malaria, babesiosis, and other blood-borne infections. Blood smears are standard but QBC serves this specific broad diagnostic utility.

qs.q: A patient infected with Wuchereria bancrofti is diagnosed with lymphatic filariasis. According to the vector-pathogen table, which mosquito species serves as the primary vector?
qs.e: Culex quinquefasciatus is listed as the primary vector for Wuchereria bancrofti transmitting lymphatic filariasis. Anopheles stephensi transmits Plasmodium vivax.

ai.summary: Filariasis is a parasitic infection that blocks lymphatic vessels, causing swelling and elephantiasis. Diagnosis relies on detecting microfilariae or antigen, and treatment uses diethylcarbamazine to kill parasites and relieve symptoms.

sections.p: Filariasis is caused by filarial nematodes, mainly Wuchereria bancrofti, transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding microfilariae in night‑time blood, antigen tests, or imaging of lymphatic obstruction.

t.b: Detects circulating microfilariae; positive confirms active infection.
Detects circulating filarial antigen; positive indicates adult worms present.
Shows lymphatic thickening or obstruction; useful when blood tests are negative.

sections.p: Staging follows the WHO classification: Stage 1 (microfilaremia), Stage 2 (lymphatic dysfunction), Stage 3 (lymphedema), Stage 4 (elephantiasis), Stage 5 (lymphangiosarcoma).
Primary cause is Wuchereria bancrofti transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Co‑factors include malnutrition, HIV, and other tropical infections that impair immunity.

t.b: High risk in endemic rural areas with stagnant water.
HIV or malnutrition increases parasite survival.

sections.p: Early symptoms are intermittent fever and night sweats. Chronic disease presents with painless swelling of lower limbs, genitalia, or breasts, progressing to skin thickening and ulceration.
Confirm infection and assess severity. When tests are unavailable, a clinical diagnosis based on exposure and typical swelling may guide empiric therapy.

t.b: Positive indicates adult worms; useful when smear is negative.
Shows lymphatic obstruction; helps stage disease.

sections.p: Complications include bacterial cellulitis, lymphangiosarcoma, and severe lymphedema leading to loss of function. Red flags are sudden swelling, fever, or ulceration.
Treat with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) to kill microfilariae and reduce inflammation. Supportive care includes hygiene, limb elevation, and compression. Avoid DEC in patients with onchocerciasis.

t.b: Kills microfilariae and enhances immune clearance; contraindicated in onchocerciasis.
Reduces swelling and prevents secondary infection.
Prevents bacterial superinfection of skin lesions.

sections.p: Regular follow‑up to monitor swelling and infection. Preventive measures include mosquito control, bed nets, and mass drug administration in endemic areas.
Chronic lymphedema from breast cancer surgery, filariasis, and other tropical infections like leprosy.
Microfilariae may be absent in chronic stages; antigen tests can be falsely negative if worm burden is low. Night‑time sampling is essential.

faq.a: Early infection can be cured with DEC; chronic lymphedema may not fully resolve but can be managed.

faq.q: Why is DEC contraindicated in onchocerciasis?
faq.a: It can trigger severe ocular damage due to immune reaction to onchocercal worms.

faq.q: What is the role of bed nets?
faq.a: They reduce mosquito bites, lowering transmission of filarial larvae.
